questions.question: The chapter's epigraph about things that cannot possibly go wrong is from which author and work?

options.text: Douglas Adams, Mostly Harmless (1992)
Terry Pratchett, Mort (1987)
Leslie Lamport, Time, Clocks and the Ordering of Events (1978)
Douglas Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach (1979)

questions.explanation: Replication looks trivially safe on paper; the chapter's point is that all the difficulty lies in handling changes to replicated data.

questions.question: Give the chapter's definition of replication.

options.text: Keeping a copy of the same data on multiple machines that are connected via a network
Splitting data across multiple machines so each holds a subset
Keeping multiple versions of the same data on one machine
Copying data between a database and a data warehouse

questions.explanation: That second option describes partitioning, which is Chapter 6.

questions.question: Which reasons does the chapter give for wanting to replicate data? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: To keep data geographically close to your users, and thus reduce latency
To allow the system to continue working even if some of its parts have failed, and thus increase availability
To scale out the number of machines that can serve read queries, and thus increase read throughput
To store more data than fits on one machine

questions.explanation: Storing more data than fits on one machine is partitioning, not replication — and this chapter explicitly assumes each machine can hold a copy of the entire dataset.

questions.question: What size assumption does Chapter 5 make, and where is it relaxed?

options.text: That the dataset is so small that each machine can hold a copy of the entire dataset; Chapter 6 relaxes it under the topic of partitioning (sharding)
That the dataset exceeds one machine; Chapter 6 relaxes it under replication
That the dataset fits in memory; Chapter 3 relaxes it
No assumption is made about size

questions.explanation: Replication and partitioning are treated as orthogonal concerns, taken one at a time.

questions.question: In which case does the chapter say replication is easy, and why?

options.text: If the data being replicated does not change over time — then you just need to copy the data to every node once, and you're done. All of the difficulty lies in handling changes to replicated data
If there is only one replica, since no coordination is needed
If replication is synchronous, since ordering is guaranteed
If the dataset is small enough to fit in memory

questions.explanation: Static data makes replication a one-off copy; mutation is what makes it an algorithm.

questions.question: Name the three replication algorithms this chapter discusses, and the chapter's claim about their coverage.

options.text: Single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication — and almost all distributed databases use one of these three approaches
Synchronous, asynchronous and semi-synchronous replication; most databases use one of the three
Statement-based, WAL shipping and logical log replication; these cover all databases
Primary-backup, chain and quorum replication; a few databases use others

questions.explanation: Those three are the chapter's organizing structure. Statement-based, WAL shipping and logical logs are implementations of the replication log, a separate axis.

questions.question: Which two example trade-offs does the chapter name, and where are they usually decided?

options.text: Whether to use synchronous or asynchronous replication, and how to handle failed replicas. These are often configuration options in databases, and although the details vary by database, the general principles are similar across many different implementations
Which consistency model to use and how many replicas to keep; these are hardcoded
Which topology to use and which conflict resolver to apply; these are chosen by the client
Whether to partition and whether to replicate; these are schema decisions

questions.explanation: Which is why the knowledge transfers between products even though the knobs are named differently.

questions.question: Replication has been studied since the 1970s and the principles haven't changed much. Why not, and why is there still so much misunderstanding?

options.text: Because the fundamental constraints of networks have remained the same. The misunderstanding persists because outside of research, many developers continued to assume for a long time that a database consisted of just one node — mainstream use of distributed databases is more recent, so many application developers are new to the area and there has been a lot of misunderstanding around issues such as eventual consistency
Because the algorithms were proven optimal; misunderstanding comes from poor documentation
Because hardware has not improved; misunderstanding comes from vendor marketing
Because the problem is undecidable; misunderstanding is inherent

questions.explanation: Network constraints are the invariant; single-node assumptions are the source of the confusion.

questions.question: Define replica, and state the question that 'inevitably arises' once you have several.

options.text: Each node that stores a copy of the database is called a replica. The question: how do we ensure that all the data ends up on all the replicas? Every write to the database needs to be processed by every replica; otherwise the replicas would no longer contain the same data
A replica is a partition of the data; the question is how to route queries
A replica is a backup; the question is how often to take one
A replica is a follower; the question is who becomes leader

questions.explanation: Every write to every replica is the constraint that all three algorithms are answers to.

questions.question: State the three steps of leader-based replication. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: One of the replicas is designated the leader; when clients want to write to the database they must send their requests to the leader, which first writes the new data to its local storage

The other replicas are followers; whenever the leader writes new data to its local storage it also sends the data change to all of its followers as part of a replication log or change stream, and each follower applies all writes in the same order as they were processed on the leader
Reads can go to the leader or any follower, but writes are only accepted on the leader — the followers are read-only from the client's point of view
Followers may accept writes as long as they forward them to the leader

questions.explanation: Same-order application on followers is what keeps the replicas consistent with the leader.

questions.question: Which alternative names does the chapter give for leader-based replication and its roles? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The scheme is also known as active/passive replication
The leader is also called the primary
Followers are also called read replicas, secondaries, or hot standbys
The scheme is also known as quorum replication

questions.explanation: A footnote on 'hot standbys' notes that different people have different definitions for hot, warm and cold standbys — in PostgreSQL a hot standby accepts reads from clients while a warm standby doesn't process any queries from clients.

questions.question: Which relational databases does the chapter list as having leader-based replication built in, with its version qualifier? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: PostgreSQL, from version 9.0 onward
MySQL
Oracle Data Guard and SQL Server's AlwaysOn Availability Groups
SQLite

questions.explanation: Beyond relational databases it is also used in MongoDB, RethinkDB and Espresso, in message brokers such as Kafka and RabbitMQ highly available queues, and in some network filesystems and replicated block devices such as DRBD — so leader-based replication is not restricted to only databases.

questions.question: Is the choice between synchronous and asynchronous replication configurable?

options.text: In relational databases this is often a configurable option; other systems are often hardcoded to be either one or the other
It is always configurable in every system
It is never configurable; it is a property of the algorithm
It is configurable only in leaderless systems

questions.explanation: A precise, hedged statement — not a universal rule.

questions.question: In Figure 5-2, replication to follower 1 is synchronous. What two things does the leader wait for confirmation before doing?

options.text: Before reporting success to the user, and before making the write visible to other clients
Before reporting success to the user, and before writing to its own local storage
Before making the write visible to other clients, and before compacting the log
Only before reporting success to the user

questions.explanation: Most readers remember only the first. Visibility to other clients is the second, and it is what makes the guarantee meaningful.

questions.question: How fast is replication 'normally', and when could a follower fall behind by several minutes or more? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Most database systems apply changes to followers in less than a second, but there is no guarantee of how long it might take
When a follower is recovering from a failure
When the system is operating near maximum capacity, or when there are network problems between the nodes
When the leader is idle

questions.explanation: Sub-second in practice, unbounded in principle.

questions.question: State the advantage and disadvantage of synchronous replication.

options.text: Advantage: the follower is guaranteed to have an up-to-date copy of the data that is consistent with the leader, so if the leader suddenly fails you can be sure the data is still available on the follower. Disadvantage: if the synchronous follower doesn't respond — because it has crashed, or there is a network fault, or any other reason — the write cannot be processed; the leader must block all writes and wait until the synchronous replica is available again
Advantage: higher write throughput. Disadvantage: possible data loss on failover
Advantage: lower latency. Disadvantage: followers may diverge
Advantage: no conflicts. Disadvantage: requires a quorum

questions.explanation: Durability guarantee bought with availability of the write path.

questions.question: Why is it impractical for all followers to be synchronous, and what is used in practice?

options.text: Because any one node outage would cause the whole system to grind to a halt. In practice, if you enable synchronous replication on a database it usually means just one of the followers is synchronous and the others are asynchronous; if the synchronous follower becomes unavailable or slow, one of the asynchronous followers is made synchronous. This configuration is sometimes called semi-synchronous
Because the leader cannot track more than one follower; in practice all followers are asynchronous
Because network bandwidth is insufficient; in practice a quorum is used
Because followers would conflict; in practice a chain is used

questions.explanation: Under semi-synchronous, at least two nodes are guaranteed to hold an up-to-date copy of the data: the leader and one synchronous follower.

questions.question: State what is lost and gained under fully asynchronous leader-based replication. Be precise about durability.

options.text: If the leader fails and is not recoverable, any writes that have not yet been replicated to followers are lost — meaning a write is not guaranteed to be durable, even if it has been confirmed to the client. The advantage is that the leader can continue processing writes even if all of its followers have fallen behind
Writes are durable but reads may be stale; the advantage is lower latency
Nothing is lost; the advantage is higher throughput
Writes are lost only if a follower fails; the advantage is simpler failover

questions.explanation: 'Even if it has been confirmed to the client' is the precise and uncomfortable part.

questions.question: Under which conditions is asynchronous replication nevertheless widely used? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Especially if there are many followers
Especially if the followers are geographically distributed
Especially if the workload is read-only
Especially if durability is the top priority

questions.explanation: Weakening durability may sound like a bad trade-off, but both conditions make synchronous replication prohibitively slow or fragile.

questions.question: What does the boxed aside on replication research name?

options.text: Chain replication, a variant of synchronous replication that has been successfully implemented in a few systems such as Microsoft Azure Storage; it also notes a strong connection between consistency of replication and consensus (getting several nodes to agree on a value), deferred to Chapter 9
Paxos replication, implemented in Google Spanner, connected to partitioning
Gossip replication, implemented in Cassandra, connected to CRDTs
Quorum replication, implemented in Riak, connected to transactions

questions.explanation: The chapter says it concentrates on the simpler forms of replication that are most commonly used in databases in practice, though data loss in asynchronous systems can be a serious problem.

questions.question: Why is simply copying data files from one node to another not sufficient for setting up a new follower?

options.text: Because clients are constantly writing to the database, so the data is always in flux — a standard file copy would see different parts of the database at different points in time, and the result might not make any sense
Because file formats differ between nodes
Because the copy would be too slow
Because file permissions would be wrong

questions.explanation: The obvious fix — locking the database to make files consistent — is rejected because it would go against the goal of high availability; setting up a follower can usually be done without downtime.

questions.question: List the four steps for setting up a new follower without downtime. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Take a consistent snapshot of the leader's database at some point in time, if possible without taking a lock on the entire database — most databases have this feature as it is also required for backups, for example innobackupex for MySQL
Copy the snapshot to the new follower node

The follower connects to the leader and requests all data changes that have happened since the snapshot was taken, which requires that the snapshot is associated with an exact position in the leader's replication log
When the follower has processed the backlog of data changes since the snapshot, we say it has caught up, and it can now continue to process changes as they happen

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL calls the log position the log sequence number; MySQL calls it binlog coordinates. How much of this is automated varies significantly by database — sometimes fully automated, sometimes an arcane multi-step workflow performed manually by an administrator.

questions.question: What surprising claim does the chapter make about why nodes go down?

options.text: That a node might go down because of an unexpected fault, but it is just as likely due to planned maintenance — for example rebooting machines to install a kernel security patch
That most outages are caused by network faults, not node faults
That hardware faults dominate all other causes
That software bugs are the most common cause

questions.explanation: Which is why the goal is to keep the system as a whole running despite individual node failures, and to keep the impact of a node outage as small as possible.

questions.question: Describe follower failure recovery, and why it is 'quite easy'.

options.text: Catch-up recovery: on its local disk each follower keeps a log of the data changes it has received from the leader, so from its log it knows the last transaction that was processed before the fault occurred. It can then connect to the leader, request all data changes that occurred during its downtime, and once it has applied them it has caught up
It must be rebuilt from a fresh snapshot every time
The leader replays its entire log from the beginning
An election is held to choose a new leader

questions.explanation: The local log gives the follower a known resume point, which is exactly what leader failure lacks.

questions.question: Failover is 'trickier'. What must happen when a leader fails? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: One of the followers needs to be promoted to be the new leader
Clients need to be reconfigured to send their writes to the new leader
The other followers need to start consuming data changes from the new leader
All data must be re-replicated from scratch

questions.explanation: Those three steps are what the chapter calls failover, which can happen manually or automatically.

questions.question: Step 1 of automatic failover is determining that the leader has failed. What mechanism is used, and what example number does the chapter give?

options.text: There is no foolproof way of detecting what has gone wrong, so most systems simply use a timeout: nodes frequently bounce messages back and forth between each other, and if a node doesn't respond for some period of time — say, 30 seconds — it is assumed to be dead. The parenthetical exception is a leader deliberately taken down for planned maintenance, where failover is intentional
A heartbeat from a central monitor; the example is 5 seconds
A consensus vote before every write; no number is given
A hardware watchdog; the example is 1 second

questions.explanation: Many things could potentially go wrong — crashes, power outages, network issues — and a timeout cannot distinguish them.

questions.question: Step 2 is choosing a new leader. What mechanisms does the chapter name, and what is this problem called?

options.text: This could be done through an election process, where the leader is chosen by a majority of the remaining replicas, or a new leader could be appointed by a previously elected controller node. The best candidate is usually the replica with the most up-to-date data changes from the old leader, to minimize any data loss. Getting all the nodes to agree on a new leader is a consensus problem, discussed in detail in Chapter 9
The longest-running replica is always chosen; this is the leader election problem
The replica with the lowest ID is chosen; this is the ordering problem
The client chooses; this is the routing problem

questions.explanation: Most-up-to-date to minimize data loss, agreed by consensus.

questions.question: Step 3 is reconfiguring the system. What is the specific danger when the old leader comes back?

options.text: It might still believe that it is the leader, not realizing that the other replicas have forced it to step down. The system needs to ensure that the old leader becomes a follower and recognizes the new leader
It will have lost all its data and must be rebuilt
It will overwrite the new leader's log automatically
It will refuse to rejoin the cluster

questions.explanation: Clients also need to send their write requests to the new leader — the chapter cross-references Request Routing.

questions.question: With asynchronous replication, what can go wrong at failover, and what is the most common solution?

options.text: The new leader may not have received all the writes from the old leader before it failed. If the former leader rejoins the cluster after a new leader has been chosen, what should happen to those writes? The new leader may have received conflicting writes in the meantime. The most common solution is for the old leader's unreplicated writes to simply be discarded, which may violate clients' durability expectations
The old leader's writes are always merged in; no data is lost
The new leader replays the old leader's log in full
The cluster refuses writes until the old leader returns

questions.explanation: Silently discarding acknowledged writes is the standard, uncomfortable resolution.

questions.question: Trace the GitHub incident the chapter describes.

options.text: An out-of-date MySQL follower was promoted to leader. The database used an autoincrementing counter to assign primary keys to new rows, and because the new leader's counter lagged behind the old leader's, it reused some primary keys that had previously been assigned by the old leader. These primary keys were also used in a Redis store, so the reuse resulted in inconsistency between MySQL and Redis, which caused some private data to be disclosed to the wrong users
A split brain caused two leaders to accept conflicting writes, corrupting the repository index
A network partition caused all writes to be lost for an hour
A failover timeout was set too short, causing repeated unnecessary failovers

questions.explanation: Discarding writes is especially dangerous if other storage systems outside of the database need to be coordinated with the database contents.

questions.question: Define split brain, and name the safety catch and its failure mode.

options.text: Split brain is when two nodes both believe that they are the leader. It is dangerous because if both leaders accept writes and there is no process for resolving conflicts, data is likely to be lost or corrupted. As a safety catch some systems have a mechanism to shut down one node if two leaders are detected — an approach known as fencing, or more emphatically Shoot The Other Node In The Head (STONITH). But if this mechanism is not carefully designed, you can end up with both nodes being shut down
Split brain is when a node loses its data; the catch is called fencing and it always works
Split brain is when followers diverge; the catch is called quorum and it can cause data loss
Split brain is when the network partitions; the catch is called STONITH and it prevents all writes

questions.explanation: The catch can overshoot and kill both nodes — fencing is discussed in more detail in Chapter 8.

questions.question: State both directions of the timeout trade-off for declaring a leader dead.

options.text: A longer timeout means a longer time to recovery in the case where the leader fails. But too short a timeout means there could be unnecessary failovers: a temporary load spike could push a node's response time above the timeout, or a network glitch could cause delayed packets. If the system is already struggling with high load or network problems, an unnecessary failover is likely to make the situation worse, not better — which is why some operations teams prefer to perform failovers manually even if the software supports automatic failover. There are no easy solutions to these problems
Longer timeouts cause unnecessary failovers; shorter timeouts delay recovery
The timeout has no effect on recovery time
Timeouts should always be as short as possible

questions.explanation: Unnecessary failover under load is a positive feedback loop, which is why manual failover survives.

questions.question: Which issues does the chapter name as 'fundamental problems in distributed systems' when closing the failover section?

options.text: Node failures; unreliable networks; and trade-offs around replica consistency, durability, availability and latency — discussed in depth in Chapter 8 and Chapter 9
Clock skew, garbage collection pauses and disk failures — discussed in Chapter 3
Conflict resolution, topology and quorum size — discussed in Chapter 6
Schema evolution, encoding and compatibility — discussed in Chapter 4

questions.explanation: The failover discussion is a preview of the distributed-systems chapters.

questions.question: Describe statement-based replication.

options.text: The leader logs every write request (statement) that it executes and sends that statement log to its followers; for a relational database, every INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE statement is forwarded to followers, and each follower parses and executes that SQL statement as if it had been received from a client
The leader sends its write-ahead log to followers, which apply it byte for byte
The leader sends row-level change records to followers
Followers poll the leader for changed rows

questions.explanation: Sending the statement rather than its effect is what makes determinism a requirement.

questions.question: Which ways can statement-based replication break down? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Nondeterministic functions — any statement calling NOW() to get the current date and time or RAND() to get a random number is likely to generate a different value on each replica

Order dependence — if statements use an autoincrementing column or depend on the existing data (such as UPDATE ... WHERE some condition), they must be executed in exactly the same order on each replica, which can be limiting when there are multiple concurrently executing transactions

Side effects — statements that have side effects such as triggers, stored procedures and user-defined functions may result in different side effects occurring on each replica, unless the side effects are absolutely deterministic
Encoding differences — statements written in one character set cannot be parsed in another

questions.explanation: Three ways, all reducible to nondeterminism.

questions.question: What is the workaround for nondeterminism, why is it not enough, and who still uses statement-based replication?

options.text: The leader can replace any nondeterministic function calls with a fixed return value when the statement is logged, so the followers all get the same value. But because there are so many edge cases, other replication methods are now generally preferred. Statement-based replication was used in MySQL before version 5.1; it is quite compact, but MySQL now switches to row-based replication if there is any nondeterminism in a statement. VoltDB uses statement-based replication and makes it safe by requiring transactions to be deterministic
Followers ask the leader for function values; MySQL still uses it exclusively
Nondeterministic functions are forbidden; only VoltDB uses statement-based replication
There is no workaround; nobody uses statement-based replication

questions.explanation: VoltDB pushes the determinism requirement up to the application, which makes the approach safe.

questions.question: What makes WAL shipping possible across both storage-engine families?

options.text: In both cases the log is an append-only sequence of bytes containing all writes to the database — in a log-structured engine the log is the main place for storage, with segments compacted and garbage-collected in the background, and in a B-tree engine every modification is first written to a write-ahead log so the index can be restored to a consistent state after a crash. So the leader can send that same log across the network and the followers build the exact same data structures
Both engines store rows in the same format
Both engines expose a logical change stream
Both engines use fixed-size pages

questions.explanation: Byte-level identity of the log is what lets the follower reconstruct byte-level identical structures — and also what couples it to the engine.

questions.question: Which databases use WAL shipping, and what is its main disadvantage?

options.text: PostgreSQL and Oracle. The main disadvantage is that the log describes the data at a very low level — which bytes were changed in which disk blocks — making replication closely coupled to the storage engine, so it is typically not possible to run different versions of the database software on the leader and the followers
MySQL and MongoDB; the disadvantage is that the log is too large
Cassandra and Riak; the disadvantage is nondeterminism
PostgreSQL and MySQL; the disadvantage is that triggers are not replicated

questions.explanation: Storage-format coupling is the cost of byte-level fidelity.

questions.question: What is the operational impact of WAL shipping's version coupling?

options.text: If the replication protocol allows the follower to use a newer software version than the leader, you can perform a zero-downtime upgrade of the database software by first upgrading the followers and then performing a failover to make one of the upgraded nodes the new leader. If the replication protocol does not allow this version mismatch, as is often the case with WAL shipping, such upgrades require downtime
Upgrades are faster but riskier
Upgrades require rebuilding all followers from snapshots
There is no operational impact; the coupling is purely theoretical

questions.explanation: What looks like a minor implementation detail costs you the zero-downtime upgrade path.

questions.question: Define a logical log, and state what a row-level record must contain in each case. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A logical log uses different log formats for replication and for the storage engine, which allows the replication log to be decoupled from the storage engine internals — 'logical' as distinct from the storage engine's physical data representation. It is usually a sequence of records describing writes to database tables at the granularity of a row
For an inserted row, the log contains the new values of all columns
For a deleted row, the log contains enough information to uniquely identify the row that was deleted — typically the primary key, or if there is no primary key, the old values of all columns
For an updated row, the log contains enough information to uniquely identify the updated row, and the new values of all columns (or at least the new values of all columns that changed)

questions.explanation: A transaction that modifies several rows generates several such log records, followed by a record indicating that the transaction was committed. MySQL's binlog, when configured to use row-based replication, uses this approach.

questions.question: Which benefits does decoupling the replication log from the storage engine give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It can more easily be kept backward compatible, allowing the leader and followers to run different versions of the database software, or even different storage engines

A logical log format is easier for external applications to parse — useful for sending database contents to an external system such as a data warehouse for offline analysis, or for building custom indexes and caches
This technique is called change data capture, returned to in Chapter 11
It reduces the size of the log by a factor of ten

questions.explanation: Version independence enables rolling upgrades; parseability enables change data capture.

questions.question: In which circumstances might you need trigger-based replication? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If you want to only replicate a subset of the data
If you want to replicate from one kind of database to another
If you need conflict resolution logic
If you need lower latency than the database's built-in replication

questions.explanation: All three require replication functionality the database doesn't provide, so it has to move up to the application layer.

questions.question: How does a trigger-based replication scheme work, and which products does the chapter name?

options.text: A trigger lets you register custom application code that is automatically executed when a data change (write transaction) occurs in a database system; the trigger can log this change into a separate table, from which it can be read by an external process that applies any necessary application logic and replicates the data change to another system. Databus for Oracle and Bucardo for Postgres work like this. Stored procedures are the alternative mechanism named alongside triggers, and Oracle GoldenGate can instead make data changes available by reading the database log
Triggers push changes directly to remote replicas over the network with no intermediate table
Triggers rewrite the WAL; the products are PostgreSQL and MySQL
Triggers are not usable for replication at all

questions.explanation: The separate table is the handoff point between the database and the external replication process.

questions.question: State the chapter's verdict on trigger-based replication.

options.text: It typically has greater overheads than other replication methods, and is more prone to bugs and limitations than the database's built-in replication — but it can nevertheless be useful due to its flexibility
It is the preferred method for most deployments
It has no overhead but is inflexible
It is faster than WAL shipping but less durable

questions.explanation: Two costs and one redeeming property.

questions.question: Describe the read-scaling architecture and its benefits.

options.text: Leader-based replication requires all writes to go through a single node, but read-only queries can go to any replica. So for a workload consisting of mostly reads and only a small percentage of writes — a common pattern on the web — you can create many followers and distribute the read requests across them. This removes load from the leader and allows read requests to be served by nearby replicas, so you can increase the capacity for serving read-only requests simply by adding more followers
Writes are distributed across replicas, increasing write throughput
Reads go only to the leader, which is cached
Both reads and writes scale linearly with the number of nodes

questions.explanation: Reads scale; writes do not. That asymmetry is inherent to single-leader replication.

questions.question: Why does the read-scaling architecture only realistically work with asynchronous replication?

options.text: Because if you tried to synchronously replicate to all followers, a single node failure or network outage would make the entire system unavailable for writing — and the more nodes you have, the likelier it is that one will be down, so a fully synchronous configuration would be very unreliable
Because synchronous replication cannot serve reads
Because asynchronous replication is always faster
Because followers cannot acknowledge writes

questions.explanation: The probability of at least one node being down grows with node count, so synchronous fan-out and read scaling are in direct conflict.

questions.question: Define eventual consistency using the chapter's construction.

options.text: A client reading from an asynchronous follower may see outdated information if the follower has fallen behind, leading to apparent inconsistencies: if you run the same query on the leader and a follower at the same time you may get different results. But this is only a temporary state — if you stop writing to the database and wait a while, the followers will eventually catch up and become consistent with the leader
All replicas are always consistent within one second
Replicas converge regardless of whether writes continue
Reads always return the most recent write

questions.explanation: The catch-up is only promised in the absence of further writes — which is what makes the guarantee so weak in a live system.

questions.question: A footnote traces the term 'eventual consistency'. What does it say?

options.text: The term was coined by Douglas Terry et al., popularized by Werner Vogels, and became the battle cry of many NoSQL projects. However, not only NoSQL databases are eventually consistent: followers in an asynchronously replicated relational database have the same characteristics
The term was coined by Werner Vogels and applies only to NoSQL databases
The term was coined by Leslie Lamport and applies only to consensus systems
The term has no traceable origin

questions.explanation: The correction matters: eventual consistency is a property of asynchronous replication, not of a product category.

questions.question: Give the chapter's magnitudes of replication lag, and its upper bound.

options.text: In practice the lag is often a fraction of a second and not noticeable; if the system is operating near capacity or there is a problem in the network, the lag can easily increase to several seconds or even minutes. As for an upper bound — there isn't one: in general there is no limit to how far a replica can fall behind
Always under one second, bounded by the replication timeout
Bounded by the configured maximum lag setting
Bounded at 30 seconds by the failover timeout

questions.explanation: Replication lag is the delay between a write happening on the leader and being reflected on a follower. 'Eventually' is deliberately vague.

questions.question: Name the three replication-lag anomalies this section covers, and the guarantee that fixes each.

options.text: Reading your own writes, fixed by read-after-write (read-your-writes) consistency; seeing things moving backward in time, fixed by monotonic reads; and violation of causality, fixed by consistent prefix reads
Stale reads, fixed by quorums; lost writes, fixed by fencing; conflicts, fixed by CRDTs
Split brain, fixed by STONITH; data loss, fixed by synchronous replication; lag, fixed by monitoring
Dirty reads, phantom reads and write skew, fixed by transaction isolation

questions.explanation: The chapter stresses these inconsistencies are not just a theoretical issue but a real problem for applications.

questions.question: Describe the setup that produces the read-your-writes anomaly.

options.text: Many applications let the user submit some data and then view what they have submitted. With asynchronous replication, if the user views the data shortly after making a write, the new data may not yet have reached the replica — so it can look to the user as though the data they submitted was lost. This is likely when new data is submitted to the leader but read from a follower, a reasonable design when data is frequently viewed but only occasionally written
It happens only when writes go to a follower
It happens only under synchronous replication
It happens only across datacenters

questions.explanation: The user's own write appearing to vanish is the most user-visible replication-lag symptom.

questions.question: State exactly what read-after-write consistency guarantees — and what it does not.

options.text: It guarantees that if the user reloads the page, they will always see any updates they submitted themselves. It makes no promises about other users: other users' updates may not be visible until some later time. It doesn't make promises about other users' updates, but it reassures the user that their own input has been saved correctly
It guarantees all users see all writes immediately
It guarantees the user sees other users' writes but not necessarily their own
It guarantees strong consistency across all replicas

questions.explanation: A per-user guarantee, not a global one.

questions.question: Describe the first implementation technique for read-after-write consistency, and its awkward precondition.

options.text: When reading something that the user may have modified, read it from the leader; otherwise read it from a follower. This requires that you have some way of knowing whether something might have been modified, without actually querying it. For example, user profile information on a social network is normally only editable by the owner of the profile, so you can always read the user's own profile from the leader and any other users' profiles from a follower
Always read from the leader, which requires no precondition
Read from the follower with the lowest lag, which requires lag monitoring
Read twice and compare, which requires idempotent reads

questions.explanation: The precondition is knowing what might be modified before you ask, which is what makes this technique brittle.

questions.question: When most things are user-editable, what are the two separate uses of 'one minute' in the alternative technique?

options.text: You could track the time of the last update and, for one minute after the last update, make all reads from the leader. And you could monitor the replication lag on followers and prevent queries on any follower that is more than one minute behind the leader
Both refer to the failover timeout
One refers to cache expiry, the other to session length
Both refer to how long the leader retains its log

questions.explanation: One is a per-user read window; the other is a per-follower eligibility threshold. Otherwise most things would have to be read from the leader, negating the benefit of read scaling.

questions.question: Describe the timestamp-remembering technique and its clock caveat.

options.text: The client can remember the timestamp of its most recent write, and the system can ensure that the replica serving any reads for that user reflects updates at least until that timestamp. If a replica is not sufficiently up to date, either the read can be handled by another replica or the query can wait until the replica has caught up. The timestamp could be a logical timestamp such as a log sequence number, or the actual system clock — in which case clock synchronization becomes critical
The server remembers each client's last write; no clocks are involved
The client polls until the data appears; no timestamps are needed
The leader stamps every read; clock skew is irrelevant

questions.explanation: Logical timestamps avoid the clock problem; wall-clock timestamps reintroduce it.

questions.question: What complexity do multiple datacenters add to read-after-write consistency?

options.text: Any request that needs to be served by the leader must be routed to the datacenter that contains the leader — which complicates the routing when replicas are spread out for geographical proximity to users or for availability
Nothing changes; each datacenter has its own leader
Timestamps become meaningless across datacenters
Reads must be served from all datacenters simultaneously

questions.explanation: Leader-directed reads turn into cross-datacenter routing decisions.

questions.question: Define cross-device read-after-write consistency and its additional issues. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If the user enters some information on one device — say a desktop web browser — and then views it on another device such as a mobile app, they should see the information they just entered

Approaches that require remembering the timestamp of the user's last update become more difficult, because the code running on one device doesn't know what updates have happened on the other device; this metadata needs to be centralized

If replicas are distributed across different datacenters there is no guarantee that connections from different devices will be routed to the same datacenter — for example if the user's computer uses the home broadband connection and their mobile device uses the cellular data network, the devices' network routes may be completely different. So if your approach requires reading from the leader, you may first need to route requests from all of a user's devices to the same datacenter
Devices cannot share a user identity, making the guarantee impossible

questions.explanation: Two issues: centralizing the metadata, and routing devices consistently.

questions.question: Trace the monotonic-reads anomaly using the chapter's user numbers.

options.text: User 2345 makes the same query twice, first to a follower with little lag and then to one with greater lag — which can happen if the user refreshes a web page and each request is routed to a random server. The first query returns a comment that was recently added by user 1234; the second query returns nothing, because the lagging follower has not yet picked up that write. In effect the second query is observing the system at an earlier point in time than the first, so time appears to go backward
User 1234 reads twice and sees the same value both times
User 2345 writes twice and the second write is lost
User 1234 reads from the leader and sees a stale value

questions.explanation: Two reads landing on differently-lagged followers is what makes time run backward for the reader.

questions.question: What subtle point does the chapter make about which outcome is actually confusing?

options.text: That it wouldn't be so bad if the first query hadn't returned anything, because the user probably wouldn't know that another user had recently added a comment. What is very confusing is to first see a comment and then see it disappear again
That missing the comment entirely is worse than seeing it disappear
That both outcomes are equally confusing
That neither outcome matters to users

questions.explanation: Ignorance is tolerable; retraction is not.

questions.question: Where does monotonic reads sit in the hierarchy, and what exactly does it rule out?

options.text: It is a lesser guarantee than strong consistency but a stronger guarantee than eventual consistency. When you read data you may see an old value; monotonic reads only means that if one user makes several reads in sequence, they will not see time go backward — they will not read older data after having previously read newer data
It is stronger than strong consistency and rules out all stale reads
It is equivalent to eventual consistency and rules out nothing
It guarantees reads always return the latest write

questions.explanation: Staleness is permitted; non-monotonicity is not.

questions.question: How is monotonic reads implemented, and what is the operational problem?

options.text: Make sure that each user always makes their reads from the same replica — for example the replica can be chosen based on a hash of the user ID rather than randomly. The problem: if that replica fails, the user's queries will need to be rerouted to another replica
Always read from the leader; the problem is leader load
Read from all replicas and take the newest; the problem is latency
Use version vectors; the problem is storage overhead

questions.explanation: Sticky routing by user hash, with failover as the weak point.

questions.question: In the consistent-prefix-reads dialog, what is the causal dependency and what does a third listener hear?

options.text: Mrs. Cake heard Mr. Poons's question and answered it — the answer is causally dependent on the question. If the things said by Mrs. Cake go through a follower with little lag but the things said by Mr. Poons have a longer replication lag, an observer sees Mrs. Cake's answer ('About ten seconds') before Mr. Poons's question. To the observer it looks as though Mrs. Cake is answering the question before Mr. Poons has even asked it — such psychic powers are impressive, but very confusing
There is no causal dependency; the observer hears both lines in order
Mr. Poons's question depends on Mrs. Cake's answer; the observer hears nothing
The dialog illustrates monotonic reads, not consistent prefix reads

questions.explanation: Figure 5-5's caption: if some partitions are replicated slower than others, an observer may see the answer before they see the question.

questions.question: State the consistent prefix reads guarantee, and where it is a particular problem.

options.text: If a sequence of writes happens in a certain order, then anyone reading those writes will see them appear in the same order. This is a particular problem in partitioned (sharded) databases: if the database always applies writes in the same order, reads always see a consistent prefix, so the anomaly cannot happen — but in many distributed databases different partitions operate independently, so there is no global ordering of writes, meaning a reader may see some parts of the database in an older state and some in a newer state
All reads return the newest write; it is a problem only in single-node databases
Reads are monotonic per user; it is a problem only across datacenters
Writes are ordered by timestamp; it is a problem only with clock skew

questions.explanation: Independent partitions without global write ordering is the structural cause.

questions.question: What two approaches does the chapter offer for consistent prefix reads?

options.text: Make sure that any writes that are causally related to each other are written to the same partition — but in some applications that cannot be done efficiently. There are also algorithms that explicitly keep track of causal dependencies, a topic returned to under the happens-before relationship and concurrency
Use a global timestamp on every write, or route all reads to the leader
Use synchronous replication, or disable partitioning
Use quorum reads, or version vectors only

questions.explanation: Co-partition the causally related writes, or track causality explicitly.

questions.question: What thought experiment does 'Solutions for Replication Lag' open with?

options.text: Think about how the application behaves if the replication lag increases to several minutes or even hours. If the answer is 'no problem', that's great. However, if the result is a bad experience for users, it's important to design the system to provide a stronger guarantee such as read-after-write. Pretending that replication is synchronous when in fact it is asynchronous is a recipe for problems down the line
Measure the average lag and set an SLA at the p99
Assume replication is synchronous and handle exceptions
Disable asynchronous replication in production

questions.explanation: The last sentence is the chapter's warning against wishful design.

questions.question: What one-sentence reason does the chapter give for the existence of transactions?

options.text: It would be better if application developers didn't have to worry about subtle replication issues and could just trust their databases to 'do the right thing' — this is why transactions exist: they are a way for a database to provide stronger guarantees so that the application can be simpler
Transactions exist to improve write throughput
Transactions exist to enable partitioning
Transactions exist to compress the replication log

questions.explanation: Framed against the cost of handling these issues in application code, which is complex and easy to get wrong.

questions.question: Many distributed databases abandoned transactions, claiming they are too expensive and eventual consistency is inevitable at scale. What does the chapter concede and reject?

options.text: There is some truth in that statement, but it is overly simplistic — the book develops a more nuanced view in Chapters 7 and 9, returning to the topic in Part III
The statement is entirely correct and transactions should be avoided
The statement is entirely wrong; transactions are always cheap
The chapter takes no position

questions.explanation: Note both halves: partial truth, overly simplistic.

questions.question: State leader-based replication's 'one major downside'.

options.text: There is only one leader, and all writes must go through it — so if you can't connect to the leader for any reason, for example due to a network interruption between you and the leader, you can't write to the database
Reads cannot be scaled
Conflicts must be resolved by the application
Followers cannot be added without downtime

questions.explanation: A footnote qualifies it: if the database is partitioned, each partition has one leader, and different partitions may have their leaders on different nodes — but each partition must nevertheless have one leader node.

questions.question: Define the multi-leader configuration, its alternative name, and the dual role each node plays.

options.text: It allows more than one node to accept writes; replication still happens in the same way, with each node that processes a write forwarding that data change to all the other nodes. It is also called active/active replication, and in it each leader simultaneously acts as a follower to the other leaders
It allows any node to accept reads but only one to accept writes; it is called read scaling
It elects a new leader per write; it is called rotating leadership
It has no leaders at all; it is called leaderless replication

questions.explanation: Every node is both leader and follower, which is what creates the conflict problem.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about multi-leader replication within a single datacenter?

options.text: It rarely makes sense to use a multi-leader setup within a single datacenter, because the benefits rarely outweigh the added complexity
It is the recommended default within a datacenter
It is required for high availability within a datacenter
It is impossible within a single datacenter

questions.explanation: Multi-leader earns its complexity only when there is a real reason for multiple write-accepting locations.

questions.question: Describe the multi-datacenter multi-leader architecture precisely.

options.text: You have a leader in each datacenter. Within each datacenter, regular leader–follower replication is used; between datacenters, each datacenter's leader replicates its changes to the leaders in other datacenters
One global leader replicates to followers in all datacenters
All nodes in all datacenters are leaders with no followers
Each datacenter has followers only, with the leader outside

questions.explanation: Two levels: leader-follower inside, leader-leader across — so you can tolerate the failure of an entire datacenter, or be closer to your users.

questions.question: How do single-leader and multi-leader compare across the chapter's three dimensions? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Performance — with single-leader, every write must go over the internet to the datacenter with the leader, adding significant latency and arguably contravening the purpose of having multiple datacenters; with multi-leader, every write can be processed in the local datacenter and replicated asynchronously, so the inter-datacenter network delay is hidden from users and perceived performance may be better

Tolerance of datacenter outages — with single-leader, if the datacenter with the leader fails, failover can promote a follower in another datacenter; with multi-leader, each datacenter can continue operating independently of the others, and replication catches up when the failed datacenter comes back online

Tolerance of network problems — traffic between datacenters usually goes over the public internet, which may be less reliable than a local network; a single-leader configuration is very sensitive to problems in this inter-datacenter link because writes are made synchronously over it, whereas a multi-leader configuration with asynchronous replication can usually tolerate network problems better, since a temporary network interruption does not prevent writes being processed
Conflict resolution — single-leader requires it, multi-leader does not

questions.explanation: The last one is inverted: multi-leader is precisely the configuration that requires conflict resolution.

questions.question: Which external tools does the chapter name for retrofitting multi-leader replication? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Tungsten Replicator for MySQL
BDR for PostgreSQL
GoldenGate for Oracle
Bucardo for Cassandra

questions.explanation: Multi-leader is sometimes built in and often bolted on by external tooling.

questions.question: What does the chapter warn about multi-leader replication being 'somewhat retrofitted'?

options.text: That because it is often implemented by external tools, features like autoincrementing keys, triggers and integrity constraints can be problematic, and there are often subtle configuration pitfalls and surprising interactions with other database features. For this reason multi-leader replication is often considered dangerous territory that should be avoided if possible
That it is slower than single-leader replication in all cases
That it cannot be used across datacenters
That it requires synchronous replication

questions.explanation: The big problem is that the same data may be concurrently modified in two different datacenters, and those write conflicts must be resolved.

questions.question: Describe the offline-operation use case for multi-leader replication.

options.text: An application that needs to continue to work while it is disconnected from the internet — for example the calendar apps on your mobile phone, laptop and other devices, where you need to see your meetings (make read requests) and enter new meetings (make write requests) at any time regardless of connectivity. Every device has a local database that acts as a leader, and there is an asynchronous multi-leader replication process (sync) between the replicas on all devices; the replication lag may be hours or even days, depending on when you have internet access
A read-only cache that syncs when online
A single-leader setup with a local follower
A leaderless store with quorum writes

questions.explanation: Each device being a leader is what makes offline writes possible.

questions.question: How does the chapter relate offline operation to multi-datacenter replication?

options.text: From an architectural point of view this setup is essentially the same as multi-leader replication between datacenters, taken to the extreme: each device is a 'datacenter', and the network connection between them is extremely unreliable. As the rich history of broken calendar sync implementations demonstrates, multi-leader replication is a tricky thing to get right. CouchDB is designed for this mode of operation
They are unrelated architectures
Offline operation is a form of leaderless replication
Offline operation is single-leader replication with a long timeout

questions.explanation: The broken-calendar-sync remark is the chapter's dry evidence that this is hard.

questions.question: What does the chapter say the local replica is in real-time collaborative editing?

options.text: With Etherpad and Google Docs, which allow multiple people to concurrently edit a text document or spreadsheet, the changes are instantly applied to the user's local replica — the state of the document in their web browser or client application — and asynchronously replicated to the server and to any other users who are editing the same document. This has a lot in common with the offline editing use case
The server holds the only replica; clients are stateless views
Each keystroke is written synchronously to the server
The local replica is a read-only cache

questions.explanation: The browser holding a writable replica is what makes this multi-leader replication.

questions.question: If you want to guarantee there will be no editing conflicts, what must the application do, and what is that equivalent to?

options.text: It must obtain a lock on the document before a user can edit it; if another user wants to edit the same document they first have to wait until the first user has committed their changes and released the lock. This collaboration model is equivalent to single-leader replication with transactions on the leader
It must use CRDTs, which is equivalent to leaderless replication
It must version every keystroke, which is equivalent to multi-leader replication
It must resolve conflicts on read, which is equivalent to quorum replication

questions.explanation: Locking eliminates concurrency, which is what single-leader replication does structurally.

questions.question: For faster collaboration you change two things. What are they, and what does that cost?

options.text: Make the unit of change very small — for example a single keystroke — and avoid locking. This allows multiple users to edit simultaneously, but it also brings all the challenges of multi-leader replication, including requiring conflict resolution
Increase the unit of change and add locking; the cost is latency
Use synchronous replication and a single leader; the cost is availability
Compress changes and batch them; the cost is bandwidth

questions.explanation: Fine-grained lock-free edits buy responsiveness and inherit every multi-leader problem.

questions.question: Trace the wiki title conflict of Figure 5-7.

options.text: User 1 changes the title from A to B and user 2 changes it from A to C at the same time. Each user's change is successfully applied to their local leader; however, when the changes are asynchronously replicated, a conflict is detected. This problem does not occur in a single-leader database
Both users write to the same leader, and the second write is rejected
User 1's write is lost before reaching any leader
The conflict is detected synchronously at write time

questions.explanation: The figure's caption: a write conflict caused by two leaders concurrently updating the same record.

questions.question: Contrast single-leader and multi-leader conflict detection, and explain why making detection synchronous is self-defeating.

options.text: In a single-leader database the second writer will either block and wait for the first write to complete, or abort the second write transaction, forcing the user to retry. In a multi-leader setup both writes are successful, and the conflict is only detected asynchronously at some later point in time — at which point it may be too late to ask the user to resolve the conflict. In principle you could make detection synchronous by waiting for the write to be replicated to all replicas before telling the user the write was successful, but by doing so you would lose the main advantage of multi-leader replication: allowing each replica to accept writes independently. If you want synchronous conflict detection, you might as well just use single-leader replication
Both detect conflicts synchronously; the difference is only in resolution
Multi-leader detects conflicts synchronously and single-leader asynchronously
Neither detects conflicts; the application must do it

questions.explanation: Synchronous detection collapses multi-leader into single-leader.

questions.question: Describe the conflict-avoidance strategy and the 'home' datacenter arrangement.

options.text: The simplest strategy for dealing with conflicts is to avoid them: if the application can ensure that all writes for a particular record go through the same leader, then conflicts cannot occur. Since many implementations of multi-leader replication handle conflicts quite poorly, avoiding conflicts is a frequently recommended approach. For example, you can ensure that requests from a particular user are always routed to the same datacenter and use the leader in that datacenter for reading and writing — different users may have different 'home' datacenters, perhaps based on geographic proximity, but from any one user's point of view the configuration is essentially single-leader
Conflicts are avoided by locking every record before writing
Conflicts are avoided by using synchronous replication
Conflicts cannot be avoided in a multi-leader setup

questions.explanation: Per-user single-leader behaviour inside a multi-leader deployment.

questions.question: Why might conflict avoidance break down? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because one datacenter has failed and you need to reroute traffic to another datacenter
Because a user has moved to a different location and is now closer to a different datacenter
Because the record's schema has changed
Because the replication topology was reconfigured to all-to-all

questions.explanation: In either situation conflict avoidance breaks down, and you have to deal with the possibility of concurrent writes on different leaders.

questions.question: In Figure 5-7, what value would each leader hold if writes were simply applied in arrival order, and why is neither order correct?

options.text: At leader 1 the title is first updated to B and then to C, ending at C; at leader 2 it is first updated to C and then to B, ending at B. That leaves the database in a permanently inconsistent state, which is not acceptable: in a replicated database values should eventually be the same in all replicas. Neither order is 'more correct' than the other, because there is no defined ordering of writes — so the database must resolve the conflict in a convergent way, meaning all replicas must arrive at the same final value when all changes have been replicated
Both leaders end at B, so there is no problem
Leader 1 ends at B and leader 2 at C; the earlier write is correct
Both end at C, which is correct because it was written second

questions.explanation: Contrast single-leader, where writes are in a sequential order and the last write determines the final value.

questions.question: Which routes to convergent conflict resolution does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Highest ID wins — give each write a unique ID such as a timestamp, long random number, UUID, or hash of the key and value, pick the write with the highest ID as the winner and throw away the other writes. If a timestamp is used, this is known as last write wins (LWW); although popular, it is dangerously prone to data loss
Highest replica number wins — give each replica a unique ID and let writes that originated at a higher-numbered replica always take precedence; this approach also implies data loss
Merge the values together — for example order them alphabetically and then concatenate them, so the merged title might be 'B/C'
Record the conflict in an explicit data structure that preserves all information, and write application code that resolves the conflict at some later time, perhaps by prompting the user

questions.explanation: Four routes, two of which the chapter explicitly flags as data-losing. LWW is discussed in detail at the end of the chapter.

questions.question: Custom conflict resolution code can execute at two moments. Describe both.

options.text: On write: as soon as the database system detects a conflict in the log of replicated changes, it calls the conflict handler — for example Bucardo allows you to write a snippet of Perl for this purpose. The handler typically cannot prompt a user, because it runs in a background process and must execute quickly. On read: all the conflicting writes are stored, and the next time the data is read, multiple versions of the data are returned to the application, which may prompt the user or automatically resolve the conflict, writing the result back to the database — CouchDB works this way
On commit and on rollback, both handled by the database
On replication and on compaction, both handled by the storage engine
Only on write; reading never surfaces conflicts

questions.explanation: The on-write constraint — background process, must be fast, cannot prompt — is what makes on-read resolution attractive.

questions.question: At what granularity does conflict resolution usually apply?

options.text: Usually at the level of an individual row or document, not for an entire transaction — so if you have a transaction that atomically makes several different writes, each write is still considered separately for the purposes of conflict resolution
At the level of the whole transaction, atomically
At the level of the whole table
At the level of the whole database

questions.explanation: Transaction atomicity does not extend to conflict resolution.

questions.question: Recount the Amazon shopping cart conflict-resolution anecdote.

options.text: Amazon is a frequently cited example of surprising effects due to a conflict resolution handler: for some time the conflict resolution logic on the shopping cart would preserve items added to the cart, but not items removed from the cart. Thus customers would sometimes see items reappearing in their carts even though they had previously been removed
Amazon lost entire carts during a datacenter failover
Amazon's handler merged carts across different customers
Amazon's handler always picked the newest cart, discarding older items

questions.explanation: An asymmetric merge — union of additions, ignoring removals — which is exactly the problem tombstones solve.

questions.question: Name the three lines of automatic conflict-resolution research. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Conflict-free replicated datatypes (CRDTs) — a family of data structures for sets, maps, ordered lists, counters and so on that can be concurrently edited by multiple users and automatically resolve conflicts in sensible ways; some have been implemented in Riak 2.0
Mergeable persistent data structures — which track history explicitly, similarly to the Git version control system, and use a three-way merge function, whereas CRDTs use two-way merges

Operational transformation — the conflict resolution algorithm behind collaborative editing applications such as Etherpad and Google Docs, designed particularly for concurrent editing of an ordered list of items, such as the list of characters that constitute a text document
Byzantine fault-tolerant merging — used in blockchain databases

questions.explanation: Implementations of these are still young, but it is likely that they will be integrated into more replicated data systems in the future, making multi-leader data synchronization much simpler for applications to deal with.

questions.question: The chapter asks 'What is a conflict?' and gives a subtle example. Why doesn't an availability check save you?

options.text: In a meeting room booking system that tracks which room is booked by which group at which time, you need to ensure each room is only booked by one group at any one time, so there must not be any overlapping bookings. A conflict can arise if two different bookings are created for the same room at the same time. Even if the application checks availability before allowing a user to make a booking, there can be a conflict if the two bookings are made on two different leaders — each leader's check passes against its own local state
The check saves you completely; no conflict is possible
The check fails because clocks are unsynchronized
The check is unnecessary because rooms are partitioned

questions.explanation: The chapter is honest that there isn't a quick ready-made answer, pointing forward to Chapter 7 and Chapter 12.

questions.question: Define replication topology, and state how many plausible topologies exist with exactly two leaders.

options.text: A replication topology describes the communication paths along which writes are propagated from one node to another. With two leaders there is only one plausible topology: leader 1 must send all of its writes to leader 2, and vice versa. With more than two leaders, various different topologies are possible
It describes the physical network wiring; with two leaders there are two topologies
It describes the partition assignment; with two leaders there are four topologies
It describes the conflict resolution order; topology count is unbounded

questions.explanation: Two leaders forces the trivial bidirectional case; complexity begins at three.

questions.question: Name the three topologies of Figure 5-8, and identify the most general and MySQL's default.

options.text: Circular, star and all-to-all. All-to-all is the most general topology, in which every leader sends its writes to every other leader. In a circular topology each node receives writes from one node and forwards those writes plus any writes of its own to one other node — MySQL by default supports only a circular topology. In a star topology one designated root node forwards writes to all of the other nodes, and the star topology can be generalized to a tree
Chain, mesh and tree; chain is the most general and MySQL's default
Circular, star and all-to-all; star is the most general and MySQL's default
Primary-backup, quorum and gossip; gossip is most general

questions.explanation: A footnote warns not to confuse the star topology with a star schema — the former describes the communication topology between nodes, the latter the structure of a data model.

questions.question: In circular and star topologies, what prevents infinite replication loops?

options.text: Each node is given a unique identifier, and in the replication log each write is tagged with the identifiers of all the nodes it has passed through. When a node receives a data change that is tagged with its own identifier, that data change is ignored, because the node knows that it has already been processed
A time-to-live counter on every write
A global sequence number assigned by the root node
A lock held while a write circulates

questions.explanation: Writes may need to pass through several nodes before they reach all replicas, so nodes must forward changes they receive from other nodes — hence the need for loop detection.

questions.question: Compare circular and star topologies with all-to-all on fault tolerance.

options.text: In circular and star topologies, if just one node fails it can interrupt the flow of replication messages between other nodes, causing them to be unable to communicate until the node is fixed. The topology could be reconfigured to work around the failed node, but in most deployments such reconfiguration would have to be done manually. The fault tolerance of a more densely connected topology such as all-to-all is better because it allows messages to travel along different paths, avoiding a single point of failure
All-to-all is worse because it has more links to fail
All three are equally fault tolerant
Star is most fault tolerant because the root can be replicated

questions.explanation: Path redundancy is what density buys.

questions.question: Trace the overtaking-writes problem of Figure 5-9 and name the general problem.

options.text: Client A inserts a row into a table on leader 1, and client B updates that row on leader 3. However, leader 2 may receive the writes in a different order: it may first receive the update — an update to a row that does not exist in the database — and only later receive the corresponding insert, which should have preceded the update. This happens because in all-to-all topologies some network links may be faster than others, for example due to network congestion, so some replication messages may 'overtake' others. The general problem is causality: the update depends on the prior insert, so we need to make sure that all nodes process the insert first and then the update
Client A and B both insert the same row, causing a duplicate key error
Leader 2 crashes and loses both writes
The writes conflict and must be merged

questions.explanation: Figure 5-9's caption: with multi-leader replication, writes may arrive in the wrong order at some replicas.

questions.question: Why don't timestamps fix Figure 5-9, and what technique is offered instead?

options.text: Simply attaching a timestamp to every write is not sufficient, because clocks cannot be trusted to be sufficiently in sync to correctly order these events at leader 2. To order these events correctly, a technique called version vectors can be used
Timestamps do fix it, provided NTP is running
Timestamps fail because they are too coarse; sequence numbers fix it
Nothing can fix it; the anomaly is unavoidable

questions.explanation: Clock skew is why causality needs logical, not physical, ordering — the topic of Detecting Concurrent Writes.

questions.question: Which two real multi-leader systems does the chapter name, and what does each fail to do?

options.text: PostgreSQL BDR does not provide causal ordering of writes, and Tungsten Replicator for MySQL doesn't even try to detect conflicts
GoldenGate loses writes and BDR duplicates them
Both fail to support circular topologies
Both fail to support multi-datacenter deployment

questions.explanation: Conflict detection techniques are poorly implemented in many multi-leader replication systems.

questions.question: What three actions does the chapter tell you to take if you use a multi-leader system? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Be aware of these issues
Carefully read the documentation
Thoroughly test your database to ensure that it really does provide the guarantees you believe it to have
Disable conflict resolution and handle it in the application

questions.explanation: Verify rather than assume — the documentation and the implementation may both overpromise.

questions.question: What do single-leader and multi-leader replication have in common, and what does leaderless replication abandon?

options.text: Both are based on the idea that a client sends a write request to one node (the leader), and the database system takes care of copying that write to the other replicas — a leader determines the order in which writes should be processed, and followers apply the leader's writes in the same order. Leaderless replication abandons the concept of a leader and allows any replica to directly accept writes from clients
Both use quorums; leaderless abandons quorums
Both are synchronous; leaderless is asynchronous
Both use conflict resolution; leaderless avoids conflicts

questions.explanation: Two properties abandoned: the leader itself, and the leader-imposed write ordering.

questions.question: Trace the history of leaderless replication.

options.text: Some of the earliest replicated data systems were leaderless, but the idea was mostly forgotten during the era of dominance of relational databases. It once again became a fashionable architecture after Amazon used it for its in-house Dynamo system
It was invented by Amazon in 2007 and had no predecessors
It originated with Cassandra and was later adopted by Amazon
It has always been the dominant architecture

questions.explanation: A footnote makes a commonly misremembered correction: Dynamo is not available to users outside of Amazon, and AWS offers a hosted database product called DynamoDB which uses a completely different architecture — it is based on single-leader replication.

questions.question: Which open source datastores have leaderless replication models inspired by Dynamo? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Riak
Cassandra
Voldemort
MongoDB

questions.explanation: Hence the label Dynamo-style. MongoDB uses leader-based replication.

questions.question: Who sends writes to the replicas in a leaderless system, and what is the crucial difference from a leader?

options.text: In some implementations the client directly sends its writes to several replicas; in others a coordinator node does this on behalf of the client — but unlike a leader database, that coordinator does not enforce a particular ordering of writes. This difference in design has profound consequences for the way the database is used
A coordinator that acts exactly like a leader, enforcing ordering
The replicas gossip among themselves; clients never write directly
A randomly elected leader per write

questions.explanation: A coordinator without ordering authority is not a leader, which is what keeps the system leaderless.

questions.question: Trace the write in Figure 5-10 with one node down.

options.text: Three replicas, one of which is unavailable — perhaps it is being rebooted to install a system update. The client (user 1234) sends the write to all three replicas in parallel; the two available replicas accept the write but the unavailable replica misses it. Say it's sufficient for two out of three replicas to acknowledge the write: after receiving two ok responses the client considers the write successful and simply ignores the fact that one of the replicas missed the write. In a leaderless configuration, failover does not exist
The write fails because one replica is down
The client waits for all three replicas before succeeding
A failover promotes a new leader, then the write proceeds

questions.explanation: Figure 5-10's caption: a quorum write, quorum read, and read repair after a node outage.

questions.question: When the unavailable node returns, what is the problem and the solution on the read path?
