options.text: Any writes that happened while the node was down are missing from that node, so if you read from it you may get stale (outdated) values as responses. To solve this, when a client reads from the database it doesn't just send its request to one replica: read requests are also sent to several nodes in parallel. The client may get different responses from different nodes — an up-to-date value from one and a stale value from another — and version numbers are used to determine which value is newer
The returning node is wiped and rebuilt from a snapshot
The returning node is excluded from reads permanently
The client reads only from the node with the highest uptime

questions.explanation: Parallel reads plus version numbers is how staleness is detected without a leader.

questions.question: Describe read repair using Figure 5-10's version numbers, and say what it works well for.

options.text: When a client makes a read from several nodes in parallel it can detect any stale responses: user 2345 gets a version 6 value from replica 3 and a version 7 value from replicas 1 and 2, so the client sees that replica 3 has a stale value and writes the newer value back to that replica. This approach works well for values that are frequently read
The client discards the stale value and does nothing further; it works for rarely-read values
The server detects staleness and repairs it in the background; it works for all values equally
The stale replica is removed from the cluster; it works for write-heavy values

questions.explanation: Read repair only fixes what gets read — which is why an anti-entropy process is also needed.

questions.question: Describe the anti-entropy process and what its absence costs.

options.text: Some datastores have a background process that constantly looks for differences in the data between replicas and copies any missing data from one replica to another. Unlike the replication log in leader-based replication, this anti-entropy process does not copy writes in any particular order, and there may be a significant delay before data is copied. Voldemort currently does not have an anti-entropy process, so without one, values that are rarely read may be missing from some replicas and thus have reduced durability — because read repair is only performed when a value is read by the application
It copies writes in order, like a replication log; all systems have one
It is the same as read repair, performed on write
It reduces durability by deleting unread values

questions.explanation: Two differences from a replication log: no ordering, and unbounded delay.

questions.question: Derive the quorum intuition from the three-replica example.

options.text: If every successful write is guaranteed to be present on at least two out of three replicas, that means at most one replica can be stale. So if you read from at least two replicas, you can be sure that at least one of the two is up to date — and if the third replica is down or slow to respond, reads can nevertheless continue returning an up-to-date value
Writing to one replica and reading from one is sufficient
You must write to all three and read from all three
Reading from one replica suffices if writes go to all three

questions.explanation: Overlap between the write set and the read set is the whole mechanism.

questions.question: State the general quorum condition with n, w and r, and explain why it works.

options.text: If there are n replicas, every write must be confirmed by w nodes to be considered successful, and we must query at least r nodes for each read. As long as w plus r is greater than n, we expect to get an up-to-date value when reading — because at least one of the r nodes we're reading from must be up to date. The set of nodes you've written to and the set you've read from must overlap, so among the r nodes there must be at least one with the latest value. Reads and writes that obey these r and w values are called quorum reads and writes: you can think of r and w as the minimum number of votes required for the read or write to be valid
As long as w plus r is less than n, reads see the latest value
As long as w equals r, reads see the latest value regardless of n
As long as w is greater than r, reads see the latest value

questions.explanation: The chapter's example values are n = 3, w = 2, r = 2. A footnote notes this kind of quorum is sometimes called a strict quorum, to contrast with sloppy quorums.

questions.question: What is the common choice of n, w and r in Dynamo-style databases, and what are the values for n = 3 and n = 5?

options.text: Make n an odd number, typically 3 or 5, and set w = r = (n + 1) / 2 rounded up — giving w = r = 2 for n = 3, and w = r = 3 for n = 5
Make n even and set w = r = n / 2 — giving 2 for n = 4
Set w = n and r = 1 always
Set w = 1 and r = n always

questions.explanation: Odd n with a simple majority is the standard configuration. A boxed note adds that you may have more than n nodes in the cluster, with any given value stored only on n nodes, which allows the dataset to be partitioned — supporting datasets larger than you can fit on one node.

questions.question: For a workload with few writes and many reads, what setting does the chapter suggest, and what is the disadvantage?

options.text: Setting w = n and r = 1, which makes reads faster; the disadvantage is that just one failed node causes all database writes to fail
Setting w = 1 and r = n, which makes writes faster with no disadvantage
Setting w = r = 1, which maximizes availability with no staleness
Setting w = r = n, which guarantees consistency at no cost

questions.explanation: It satisfies the quorum condition (n plus 1 is greater than n) but concentrates all the fragility on the write path.

questions.question: Which statements about the quorum condition's tolerance are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If w is less than n, we can still process writes if a node is unavailable; if r is less than n, we can still process reads if a node is unavailable
With n = 3, w = 2, r = 2 we can tolerate one unavailable node; with n = 5, w = 3, r = 3 we can tolerate two unavailable nodes

Normally reads and writes are always sent to all n replicas in parallel — w and r determine how many nodes we wait for, that is, how many of the n nodes need to report success before we consider the read or write to be successful
Reads and writes are sent only to w or r nodes respectively, chosen at random

questions.explanation: The last one is the mistake readers most often make: w and r are waiting thresholds, not sending counts.

questions.question: If fewer than w or r nodes are available, what happens — and does the reason for unavailability matter?

options.text: Writes or reads return an error. A node could be unavailable because it is down (crashed, powered down), because of an error executing the operation (can't write because the disk is full), because of a network interruption between the client and the node, or for any number of other reasons. We only care whether the node returned a successful response and don't need to distinguish between different kinds of fault
The operation blocks until enough nodes return; the reason determines the retry policy
The operation succeeds with a warning; only crashes count as unavailable
The coordinator substitutes another node automatically; the reason is logged

questions.explanation: Deliberate indifference to fault type is what keeps the quorum model simple.

questions.question: Why are r and w often chosen to be a majority, and what does the chapter insist about quorums in general?

options.text: Because a majority (more than n/2) ensures that w plus r is greater than n while still tolerating up to n/2 node failures. But quorums are not necessarily majorities: it only matters that the sets of nodes used by the read and write operations overlap in at least one node. Other quorum assignments are possible, which allows some flexibility in the design of distributed algorithms
Because majorities are required by the quorum theorem; no other assignment is valid
Because majorities minimize latency; other assignments are always worse
Because majorities guarantee strong consistency in all cases

questions.explanation: Overlap, not majority, is the actual requirement.

questions.question: What happens if you deliberately set w plus r to be less than or equal to n?

options.text: Reads and writes will still be sent to n nodes, but a smaller number of successful responses is required for the operation to succeed. You are then more likely to read stale values, because it's more likely that your read didn't include the node with the latest value. On the upside, this configuration allows lower latency and higher availability: if many replicas become unreachable there is a higher chance that you can continue processing reads and writes. Only after the number of reachable replicas falls below w or r does the database become unavailable for writing or reading, respectively
The database refuses the configuration as invalid
Reads are still guaranteed fresh but writes may be lost
Latency increases and availability decreases

questions.explanation: A deliberate trade of freshness for latency and availability.

questions.question: Even with w plus r greater than n, stale values can be returned. Which scenarios does the chapter give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Sloppy quorum — the w writes may end up on different nodes than the r reads, so there is no longer a guaranteed overlap between the r nodes and the w nodes

Concurrent writes — if two writes occur concurrently it is not clear which one happened first; the only safe solution is to merge the concurrent writes, and if a winner is picked based on a timestamp (last write wins), writes can be lost due to clock skew. A write concurrent with a read may be reflected on only some of the replicas, in which case it is undetermined whether the read returns the old or the new value

A partially failed write — if a write succeeded on some replicas but failed on others (for example because the disks on some nodes are full) and overall succeeded on fewer than w replicas, it is not rolled back on the replicas where it succeeded; so although the write was reported as failed, subsequent reads may or may not return the value from that write

Restore from an old replica — if a node carrying a new value fails and its data is restored from a replica carrying an old value, the number of replicas storing the new value may fall below w, breaking the quorum condition. Plus unlucky timing edge cases

questions.explanation: Six scenarios in all; note the deliberate hedge in the partially-failed-write case — 'may or may not'.

questions.question: What does the chapter concede and deny about quorum guarantees?

options.text: Quorums appear to guarantee that a read returns the latest written value, but in practice it is not so simple. Dynamo-style databases are generally optimized for use cases that can tolerate eventual consistency; the parameters w and r allow you to adjust the probability of stale values being read, but it is wise to not take them as absolute guarantees. In particular you usually do not get the guarantees discussed under Problems with Replication Lag — reading your writes, monotonic reads, or consistent prefix reads — so stronger guarantees generally require transactions or consensus
Quorums guarantee strong consistency in all configurations
Quorums provide monotonic reads and read-your-writes automatically
Quorums provide no guarantees whatsoever

questions.explanation: Note the word 'probability' — that is the honest description of what w and r buy you.

questions.question: How do you compute replication lag in a leader-based system, and what makes the computation possible?

options.text: The database typically exposes metrics for the replication lag, which you can feed into a monitoring system. This is possible because writes are applied to the leader and to followers in the same order, and each node has a position in the replication log — the number of writes it has applied locally — so by subtracting a follower's current position from the leader's you can measure the lag
By comparing wall-clock timestamps on each node
By counting the rows on each node and taking the difference
It cannot be measured, only estimated

questions.explanation: A single ordered log gives every node a scalar position, which is what makes subtraction meaningful. If a follower falls behind significantly the monitoring should alert you, which may indicate a problem in the network or an overloaded node.

questions.question: Why is monitoring staleness harder without a leader? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because in leaderless replication there is no fixed order in which writes are applied, so there is no single log position to compare
Because if the database only uses read repair with no anti-entropy process, there is no limit to how old a value might be — a value that is infrequently read may be ancient
Because leaderless databases have no version numbers
Because clients cannot read from more than one replica

questions.explanation: There has been research on measuring replica staleness and predicting the expected percentage of stale reads depending on the parameters n, w and r — the chapter cites Bailis, Venkataraman, Franklin et al. on quantifying eventual consistency with PBS — but this is not yet common practice. The chapter's wish: eventual consistency is a deliberately vague guarantee, but for operability it's important to be able to quantify 'eventual'.

questions.question: Which benefits do properly configured quorums provide? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They let a database tolerate the failure of individual nodes without the need for failover
They tolerate individual nodes going slow, because requests don't have to wait for all n nodes to respond — they can return when w or r nodes have responded
They suit use cases that require high availability and low latency, and that can tolerate occasional stale reads
They guarantee no stale reads under all circumstances

questions.explanation: Failure and slowness tolerance without failover, for workloads that can accept occasional staleness.

questions.question: What fault motivates sloppy quorums, and what is odd about the nodes' status?

options.text: A network interruption can easily cut off a client from a large number of database nodes. Although those nodes are alive, and other clients may be able to connect to them, to a client that is disconnected from them they might as well be dead — in which case fewer than w or r reachable nodes remain, and the client can no longer reach a quorum. In a large cluster with significantly more than n nodes, the client can probably connect to some database nodes, just not to the nodes that it needs to assemble a quorum for a particular value
All nodes have crashed, so no quorum is possible
The disks are full, so writes fail
The clocks have drifted, so ordering is impossible

questions.explanation: Alive but unreachable is the specific condition sloppy quorums address.

questions.question: Define sloppy quorum and hinted handoff, with the chapter's analogy.

options.text: A sloppy quorum means writes and reads still require w and r successful responses, but those may include nodes that are not among the designated n 'home' nodes for a value. Once the network interruption is fixed, any writes that one node temporarily accepted on behalf of another node are sent to the appropriate 'home' nodes — this is called hinted handoff. The analogy: if you lock yourself out of your house you may knock on the neighbor's door and ask whether you may stay on their couch temporarily; once you find your keys again, your neighbor politely asks you to get off their couch and go home
A sloppy quorum reduces w and r below the required threshold; hinted handoff retries failed writes
A sloppy quorum writes to fewer than w nodes; hinted handoff is a background repair
A sloppy quorum elects a temporary leader; hinted handoff demotes it

questions.explanation: The count is preserved; the membership of the set is relaxed.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say a sloppy quorum isn't a quorum at all?

options.text: Because it is useful for increasing write availability — as long as any w nodes are available the database can accept writes — but it means that even when w plus r is greater than n you cannot be sure to read the latest value for a key, since the latest value may have been temporarily written to some nodes outside of n. Thus a sloppy quorum actually isn't a quorum at all in the traditional sense: it's only an assurance of durability, namely that the data is stored on w nodes somewhere, with no guarantee that a read of r nodes will see it until the hinted handoff has completed
Because it uses fewer than w nodes
Because it does not increase availability at all
Because it guarantees only freshness, not durability

questions.explanation: Durability without overlap — the read set and write set may now be disjoint.

questions.question: Are sloppy quorums optional, and what are the defaults?

options.text: They are optional in all common Dynamo implementations: in Riak they are enabled by default, and in Cassandra and Voldemort they are disabled by default
They are mandatory in all three systems
They are enabled by default in all three
They are disabled by default in all three

questions.explanation: Riak differs from Cassandra and Voldemort on the default.

questions.question: How do Cassandra and Voldemort handle multi-datacenter operation?

options.text: Within the normal leaderless model: the number of replicas n includes nodes in all datacenters, and in the configuration you can specify how many of the n replicas you want to have in each datacenter. Each write from a client is sent to all replicas regardless of datacenter, but the client usually only waits for acknowledgment from a quorum of nodes within its local datacenter — so it is unaffected by delays and interruptions on the cross-datacenter link. The higher-latency writes to other datacenters are often configured to happen asynchronously
They keep all communication local to one datacenter and replicate asynchronously between clusters
They require a quorum spanning all datacenters for every write
They elect a leader per datacenter

questions.explanation: Riak differs: it keeps all communication between clients and database nodes local to one datacenter, so n describes the number of replicas within one datacenter, and cross-datacenter replication between database clusters happens asynchronously in the background, similar to multi-leader replication. Leaderless replication suits multi-datacenter operation because it is designed to tolerate conflicting concurrent writes, network interruptions and latency spikes.

questions.question: Conflicts occur in Dynamo-style stores 'even if strict quorums are used'. On which additional occasions can they arise?

options.text: During read repair or hinted handoff
During compaction or snapshotting
During failover or leader election
Only when clients write concurrently; there are no other occasions

questions.explanation: Both are mechanisms that move values between nodes outside the normal write path, so both can introduce conflicts.

questions.question: Trace Figure 5-12 node by node.

options.text: Two clients, A and B, simultaneously write to key X in a three-node datastore. Node 1 receives the write from A but never receives the write from B due to a transient outage. Node 2 first receives the write from A, then the write from B. Node 3 first receives the write from B, then the write from A. If each node simply overwrote the value whenever it received a write, node 2 would think the final value of X is B whereas the other nodes would think the value is A — and the nodes would become permanently inconsistent
All three nodes receive both writes in the same order, ending consistent
Node 1 receives both, nodes 2 and 3 receive neither
The writes are serialized by a coordinator, so no inconsistency arises

questions.explanation: Figure 5-12's caption: concurrent writes in a Dynamo-style datastore, where there is no well-defined ordering. Events may arrive in a different order at different nodes due to variable network delays and partial failures.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about database implementations' conflict handling, and what obligation does that place on you?

options.text: In order to become eventually consistent the replicas should converge toward the same value. One might hope that replicated databases would handle this automatically, but unfortunately most implementations are quite poor: if you want to avoid losing data, you — the application developer — need to know a lot about the internals of your database's conflict handling
All implementations handle conflicts correctly, so no work is needed
Conflict handling is entirely the database's responsibility
Conflicts cannot be avoided, so data loss is inevitable

questions.explanation: An unusually blunt transfer of responsibility to the application developer.

questions.question: Describe last write wins and the two products' stance on it.

options.text: Declare that each replica need only store the most 'recent' value and allow 'older' values to be overwritten and discarded; provided we have a way of unambiguously determining which write is more 'recent' and every write is eventually copied to every replica, the replicas will eventually converge to the same value. We can attach a timestamp to each write, pick the biggest timestamp as the most recent, and discard any writes with an earlier timestamp. LWW is the only supported conflict resolution method in Cassandra, and an optional feature in Riak
Merge all concurrent values; mandatory in Riak, optional in Cassandra
Pick the lowest timestamp; optional in both
Store all versions as siblings; mandatory in Cassandra

questions.explanation: Since neither client knew about the other one, it's not clear which happened first — it doesn't really make sense to say that either happened 'first': we say the writes are concurrent, so their order is undefined. The ordering LWW imposes is arbitrary.

questions.question: State the cost of LWW, including the claim most readers miss.

options.text: It achieves eventual convergence, but at the cost of durability: if there were several concurrent writes to the same key, even if they were all reported as successful to the client because they were written to w replicas, only one of the writes will survive and the others will be silently discarded. Moreover, LWW may even drop writes that are not concurrent
It only discards writes that are genuinely concurrent
It never discards writes, only reorders them
It costs nothing; convergence is free

questions.explanation: So LWW is not merely lossy for concurrent writes — clock skew can make it lose non-concurrent ones too.

questions.question: What is the only safe way to use a database with LWW?

options.text: Ensure that a key is only written once and thereafter treated as immutable, thus avoiding any concurrent updates to the same key — for example a recommended way of using Cassandra is to use a UUID as the key, thus giving each write operation a unique key. There are some situations, such as caching, in which lost writes are perhaps acceptable; if losing data is not acceptable, LWW is a poor choice for conflict resolution
Synchronize all clocks with NTP and use wall-clock timestamps
Use LWW only for reads, not writes
Set w equal to n so all replicas agree

questions.explanation: Write-once immutable keys make concurrency structurally impossible.

questions.question: Define the happens-before relationship and concurrency as the chapter does.

options.text: An operation A happens before another operation B if B knows about A, or depends on A, or builds upon A in some way. Two operations are concurrent if neither happens before the other — that is, neither knows about the other. For any two operations there are three possibilities: A happened before B, B happened before A, or A and B are concurrent. If one operation happened before another, the later operation should overwrite the earlier operation; if the operations are concurrent, we have a conflict that needs to be resolved
A happens before B if A's timestamp is smaller; concurrency means equal timestamps
A happens before B if A was sent from a lower-numbered node; concurrency means same node
A happens before B if A committed first; concurrency is impossible in a distributed system

questions.explanation: Knowledge, not time, is the criterion — the chapter cites Lamport's Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System. Whether one operation happens before another is the key to defining what concurrency means.

questions.question: Which of the chapter's earlier figures is concurrent and which is not?

options.text: Figure 5-9 is not concurrent: A's insert happens before B's increment, because the value incremented by B is the value inserted by A — B's operation builds upon A's, so B is causally dependent on A. Figure 5-12 is concurrent: neither client knows that another client is also performing an operation on the same key, so there is no causal dependency between the operations
Figure 5-9 is concurrent and Figure 5-12 is not
Both are concurrent
Neither is concurrent

questions.explanation: Causal dependency in one, mutual ignorance in the other.

questions.question: The 'Concurrency, Time, and Relativity' box makes a counterintuitive claim. What is it?

options.text: It may seem that two operations should be called concurrent if they occur 'at the same time', but in fact it is not important whether they literally overlap in time — exact time doesn't matter: we simply call two operations concurrent if they are both unaware of each other, regardless of the physical time at which they occurred. In the special theory of relativity, information cannot travel faster than the speed of light, so two events some distance apart cannot possibly affect each other if the time between them is shorter than the time light takes to travel that distance. In computer systems two operations might be concurrent even though the speed of light would in principle have allowed one to affect the other: if the network was slow or interrupted at the time, two operations can occur some time apart and still be concurrent, because network problems prevented one operation from being able to know about the other
That concurrency is defined purely by wall-clock overlap
That relativity makes concurrency impossible to define
That the speed of light sets the minimum replication lag

questions.explanation: Computer systems are more permissive about concurrency than physics, because the network can fail to deliver knowledge even when light had time to.

questions.question: In Figure 5-13's shopping cart, what does the server do on write 3 when client 1 adds flour with version number 1?

options.text: The client sends the value [milk, flour] with version number 1, so the server knows it supersedes the prior value of [milk] but is concurrent with [eggs]; it assigns version 3, overwrites the version 1 value [milk], and keeps the version 2 value [eggs] — leaving server state [milk, flour] at v3 and [eggs] at v2
It overwrites both [milk] and [eggs], leaving only [milk, flour]
It rejects the write because version 1 is stale
It keeps all three values as siblings

questions.explanation: The version number tells the server exactly which prior state the write is based on, so it can distinguish overwrites from concurrent values. If the shopping cart example strikes you as too inane, the chapter suggests imagining instead two air traffic controllers concurrently adding aircraft to the sector they are tracking.

questions.question: What does Figure 5-14 add, and what observations does the chapter draw from it?

options.text: It illustrates the dataflow between the operations of Figure 5-13 as a graph of causal dependencies, where the arrows indicate which operation happened before which other operation, in the sense that the later operation knew about or depended on the earlier one. Two observations: the client is never fully up to date with the data on the server, since there is always another operation going on concurrently — but old versions of the value do get overwritten eventually, and no writes are lost
It shows the physical network topology, proving all writes were serialized
It shows wall-clock timestamps, proving the writes were not concurrent
It shows that some writes are lost, which is unavoidable

questions.explanation: Never fully current, but never lossy — the two properties the algorithm buys.

questions.question: State the rules of the version-number algorithm. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The server maintains a version number for every key, increments it every time that key is written, and stores the new version number along with the value written
When a client reads a key, the server returns all values that have not been overwritten, as well as the latest version number. A client must read a key before writing

When a client writes a key it must include the version number from the prior read, and it must merge together all values that it received in the prior read (the response from a write request can be like a read, returning all current values, which allows chaining several writes)

When the server receives a write with a particular version number, it can overwrite all values with that version number or below — since it knows they have been merged into the new value — but it must keep all values with a higher version number, because those are concurrent with the incoming write

questions.explanation: Crucially, the server can determine whether two operations are concurrent by looking at the version numbers — it does not need to interpret the value itself, so the value could be any data structure. A write without a version number is concurrent with all other writes, so it will not overwrite anything and will just be returned as one of the values on subsequent reads.

questions.question: Riak calls concurrent values siblings. Merging the two final siblings of Figure 5-14, what is the result and what detail does the chapter point out?

options.text: Merging [milk, flour, eggs, bacon] and [eggs, milk, ham] by union gives [milk, flour, eggs, bacon, ham] without duplicates — and note that milk and eggs appear in both siblings even though they were each only written once
The merge yields [eggs, milk, ham] because it has the higher version
The merge duplicates milk and eggs, giving seven items
The siblings cannot be merged without losing data

questions.explanation: This is essentially the same problem as conflict resolution in multi-leader replication: you could pick one value based on a version number or timestamp (last write wins), but that implies losing data, so you may need to do something more intelligent in application code. The algorithm ensures that no data is silently dropped, at the cost of requiring clients to clean up afterward by merging the concurrently written values.

questions.question: Where does union merging break, and what is the fix called?

options.text: It breaks if you want to allow people to also remove things from their carts, not just add things: if you merge two sibling carts and an item has been removed in only one of them, the removed item will reappear in the union of the siblings. So an item cannot simply be deleted from the database when it is removed — instead the system must leave a marker with an appropriate version number to indicate that the item has been removed when merging siblings. Such a deletion marker is known as a tombstone, familiar from log compaction in Chapter 3
It breaks on additions; the fix is a version vector
It breaks on updates; the fix is last write wins
It does not break; union merging is always correct

questions.explanation: Merging siblings in application code is complex and error-prone, so Riak's CRDT datatype support can automatically merge siblings in sensible ways, including preserving deletions.

questions.question: Why is a single version number insufficient with multiple replicas, and what replaces it?

options.text: A single version number to capture dependencies between operations is not sufficient when there are multiple replicas accepting writes concurrently. Instead we need to use a version number per replica as well as per key: each replica increments its own version number when processing a write and also keeps track of the version numbers it has seen from each of the other replicas, which tells it which values to overwrite and which to keep as siblings. The collection of version numbers from all the replicas is called a version vector
A single version number is sufficient; version vectors are an optimization
Timestamps replace version numbers when there are multiple replicas
A global counter replaces the per-key version number

questions.question: Name the interesting version vector variant, the system using it, and Riak's name for the encoded form.

options.text: The dotted version vector, used in Riak 2.0. Version vectors are sent from the database replicas to clients when values are read, and need to be sent back to the database when a value is subsequently written — quite similar to the shopping cart example. Riak encodes the version vector as a string that it calls causal context, and it allows the database to distinguish between overwrites and concurrent writes
The vector clock, used in Cassandra; Riak calls the encoding a digest

questions.question: What cross-replica operation do version vectors make safe, and what is the caveat?

options.text: The version vector structure ensures that it is safe to read from one replica and subsequently write back to another replica. Doing so may result in siblings being created, but no data is lost as long as siblings are merged correctly — and like in the single-replica example, the application may need to merge siblings
They make it safe to write to any replica with no siblings ever created

They eliminate the need for application-level merging

questions.question: Which purposes does the summary say replication can serve? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: High availability — keeping the system running even when one machine, or several machines, or an entire datacenter goes down
